lines.say: Your app found one user out of a hundred million in the blink of an eye. It skipped almost all the others.
lines.show: Your app found *one user* out of *100 million* in the blink of an eye. It skipped almost all the others.

lines.say: Your users live in a table, one row each. Without help, the database may check every row until it finds yours. With millions of rows, that's slow.
lines.show: Your users live in a table, *one row each.* Without help, the database may check *every row* until it finds yours. With millions of rows, that's [slow.]

lines.say: An index fixes that. A common one keeps a single column, like emails, sorted, and each entry points to that user's row.
lines.show: An [index] fixes that. A common one keeps a single column, like emails, *sorted,* and each entry points to that user's row.

lines.say: Because it's sorted, the database narrows it down in a few steps. Like a book's index: find the word, get the page, skip the rest.
lines.show: Because it's sorted, the database narrows it down in *a few steps.* Like a book's index: find the word, get the page, [skip the rest.]

lines.say: One catch. Every index takes space, and every new row has to update it too. So index the columns you search by, not everything.
lines.show: One catch. Every index takes *space,* and every new row has to *update it too.* So index the columns [you search by,] not everything.

lines.say: Postgres and MySQL automatically index your primary key, usually the ID.
lines.show: *Postgres* and *MySQL* automatically index your *primary key,* usually the ID.
